hints: Apply integration by parts twice, first choosing $u=x^2$ and $dv=\cos2x\,dx$.
This gives a boundary term involving $x^2\sin2x$ and a remaining integral $\int x\sin2x\,dx$.
Integrate the remaining product by parts to obtain an antiderivative containing $x^2\sin2x$, $x\cos2x$, and $\sin2x$.
Evaluate at $x=\pi/4$ and $x=0$ using exact trigonometric values, then simplify to the stated form.
walkthrough:
Use integration by parts $\int u v' = uv - \int u' v$ on $\int x^2\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$:
Let $u = x^2 \implies u' = 2x$, and $v' = \cos 2x \implies v = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x$:
$$\int x^2\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = x^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right) - \int (2x)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right)\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 2x - \int x\sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Apply integration by parts to the remaining integral $\int x\sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$:
Let $u = x \implies u' = 1$, and $v' = \sin 2x \implies v = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x$:
$$\int x\sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = x\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right) - \int 1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right)\mathrm{d}x$$
$$= -\dfrac{1}{2}x\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\int \cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$$
$$= -\dfrac{1}{2}x\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2x$$

Combine the two integration steps to write the complete antiderivative:
$$\int x^2\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 2x - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}x\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2x\right)$$
$$= \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}x\cos 2x - \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2x$$

Set up the limits of integration from $0$ to $\dfrac{1}{4}\pi$:
$$\left[\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}x\cos 2x - \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{1}{4}\pi}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$:
$$2x = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi \implies \sin 2x = \sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right) = 1, \quad \cos 2x = \cos\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right) = 0$$
$$x^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi^2}{16}$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi: \quad \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi^2}{16}\right)(1) + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right)(0) - \dfrac{1}{4}(1) = \dfrac{\pi^2}{32} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{\pi^2 - 8}{32}$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $x = 0$:
$$\text{At } x = 0: \quad \dfrac{1}{2}(0)^2(0) + \dfrac{1}{2}(0)(1) - \dfrac{1}{4}(0) = 0$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\text{Integral} = \dfrac{\pi^2 - 8}{32} - 0 = \dfrac{1}{32}(\pi^2 - 8)$$
This proves the required result.
